To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

neighborhood racial composition and neighborhood socioeconomic status are associated differently with odds of triple negative breast cancer diagnosis in Black women compared with White women, and that the relationships differ by age.

neighborhood racial and socioeconomic composition are associated with the odds of TNBC diagnosis relative to HR+HER2− breast cancer among Black and White breast cancer survivors, and that these relationships differ across women’s race groups and by women’s age at diagnosis.

we found modestly higher odds of triple-negative (vs. hormone receptor-positive/ HER2-negative) breast cancer subtype among Black women in higher-income neighborhoods, but no such association for White women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
racial disparities in breast cancer subtypes, specifically triple-negative breast cancer, among Black and White American women.
the role that neighborhood socioeconomic and racial characteristics play in Black–White disparities in triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype with poorer prognosis.
the relationship between the social environment, as defined by neighborhood-level characteristics, and breast cancer subtype.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neighborhood racial composition and income are not associated with odds of TNBC in White women, but are associated with odds in Black women, with the greatest reduction among those diagnosed at ≥ 65.

the associations between breast cancer subtype, neighborhood socioeconomic status and racial composition differ by race and that racial and social patterning of breast cancer subtypes warrants further investigation.
the associations between neighborhood composition, socioeconomic status and odds of triple negative breast cancer subtype differ by race and by age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Black women with breast cancer who are older or have lower socioeconomic status are more likely to have the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer, which is more difficult to treat and more likely to be fatal.

the odds of TNBC are reduced in neighborhoods with higher income and higher percentages Black among Black women, and that the odds of triple-negative subtype are reduced among Black women with higher income, and White women with higher income in neighborhoods with a larger Black population.
neighborhood-level racial and socioeconomic factors are associated with breast cancer subtype in Black and White women, and the magnitude of these associations varies across race and age groups.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the relationship between neighborhood racial/ethnic and socioeconomic composition and TNBC subtype differs across racial groups, suggesting that racial/ethnic disparities in breast cancer may be driven in part by differences in social context.

the relationships between neighborhood composition and breast cancer subtype vary by race and age, and that racial composition and socioeconomic status may have differential impacts on breast cancer subtypes in the Black population.
neighborhood-level socioeconomic and racial composition may be important to consider when studying breast cancer subtype differences among Black and White U.S. women.
